title: The task layer under the missions
summary: A mission in Supermarket Simulator is not one job: the game has named tasks underneath it, covering filling, closing and delivering an order, an interaction at the scale, ice-cream requests with a display and pictures of their own, and a container that holds progression.
body: Missions are built on tasks. The game keeps a task of its own alongside the mission, the container and the system, which is why a mission can be made of several steps rather than being a single instruction.

Order work is named in three parts: filling an order, closing it and delivering it. They are separate jobs rather than one job of handling an order, which is why an order can be part-finished without being finished.
The scale has an interaction task of its own, so weighing something is a job the game can hand out rather than only an action you perform when you get there.

Ice cream has requests of its own. A request is an object of its own, it has a display, and it has a generator that makes the pictures on it, which is why an order for ice cream can be shown rather than described.
Progression is kept in a container, which is how the game can hold what has been unlocked and what has not without every screen keeping a copy of its own.
Teaching jobs are shown by a display of their own, so a tutorial objective and a mission task are told apart by what shows them rather than by what they ask for.
What this entry does not tell you: how many tasks a mission holds, what a task pays, or how progression is counted. We have not verified those points, so we do not print them.

facts.claim: A mission is built on tasks of its own rather than being a single instruction.
Order work is three named tasks: filling, closing and delivering.
The scale has an interaction task of its own.
An ice-cream request is an object with a display and a generator for its pictures.
Progression is kept in a container of its own.
A teaching job is shown by a display of its own.
